summary:
Ingushetia stands under Russia's national framework: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. Its advisory records surveillance of foreign nationals and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused. Since January 2024, organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as extremist. The Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. Activity associated with the extremist designation exposes LGBT+ people to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, and organisers to 6 to 10 years.
tangentialFactors:
Global Affairs Canada lists Ingushetia among the republics experiencing frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai, and pairs that listing with its avoid-all-travel advice for Russia as a whole.

The UK Home Office policy note records that violence tied to the extremist designation is spreading beyond the North Caucasus, so the regional pattern a visitor observes is not contained by the republic's borders.

The same note frames the North Caucasus as an exception to an assessment that otherwise finds no persecution for LGBT+ people elsewhere in Russia. The heightened standard therefore attaches to this region specifically, including for the purposes of an asylum claim brought from it.
localsOnly:
David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.

The UK Home Office policy note documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people running from 2017 through 2024, which form the evidentiary basis for its persecution finding on residents of the North Caucasus.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records prosecutions, raids or other enforcement actions taken inside Ingushetia itself. The republic-level picture rests on regional testimony from a support organisation and on a foreign asylum policy note, neither of which reports Ingushetia-specific case counts.

The UK Home Office findings quoted here are from the June 2025 version of its country policy note; whether later revisions retained the North Caucasus exception is not established by the sources in hand.

The Ministry of Interior's requirement of special permission to enter certain areas is stated without naming those areas or describing the application process, so a visitor cannot determine from this inventory which zones are restricted or how clearance is obtained.

Local practice in applying Russia's 2023 gender-recognition and document rules within Ingushetia is not separately sourced; the national statute governs, but no republic-level evidence of how it is administered is available here.
